articles.title: The territorial rights of wild animals: Justification
articles.abstract: Territorial rights (TR) have become foundational in normative political theory, addressing pressing questions about boundary drawing, governance, and resource use. Influential TR theorists Cara Nine and Margaret Moore justify humans’ TR based on the functional, social, and identity‐anchored normative significance of non‐substitutable places. However, these arguments treat animals as resources, excluding them from normative consideration and political standing. This article analyzes Nine and Moore's arguments to assess whether their justificatory logic applies to wild animals. Using mule deers as a case study, I test whether they have sufficiently weighty interests in occupancy, residency, resource use, and control to ground duties on humans and whether TR theories should continue to treat animals as mere natural resources.

articles.title: Measuring Partisanship and Representation in Online Congressional Communications
articles.authors: MICHAEL KISTNER, MICHAEL HESELTINE, ROBERT ALVAREZ, MAYA FITCH, LUCAS LOTHAMER, ELIZABETH SIMAS
articles.abstract: Social media and the internet have created new ways for representatives to communicate. How have members of Congress responded to these opportunities? We introduce a multi-platform dataset of congressional communications extending back to the onset of the social media era. Using computational language processing, we classify approximately 4.7 million tweets, 2.4 million Facebook posts, and 184,000 email newsletters authored by members of Congress between 2009 and 2022 based on intended purpose, and scale the partisanship of each message along a continuous left–right dimension. After validation, we demonstrate how our data can be used to study partisanship and representation in the contemporary Congress. Importantly, our data show congressional rhetoric has become more partisan and negative as social media usage has increased. We identify one potential mechanism contributing to this trend: partisanship and negativity receive inflated levels of positive engagement on social media relative to other forms of messaging like credit claiming or constituency service.

articles.title: Are Voters Myopic or Looking for Improvement?
articles.abstract: Timing of valence outcomes plays an important role in key theories of electoral choice, and different models place different emphases on past and future outcomes. Whereas sanctioning models consider only retrospective evaluations as an accountability mechanism, selection models hold that voters use past and proposed future conditions to infer the incumbent’s ability to deliver benefits. Drawing on four surveys run on six different samples, we demonstrate that voters prefer improving conditions in both retrospection and prospection. In retrospection, this pattern is difficult to distinguish from overweighting of temporally proximate conditions, which gave rise to the notion of “the myopic voter.” Distinguishing the two processes, we find that people do not ignore early datapoints and reward improving conditions (in both retrospection and prospection). This preference for improvement does not simply reflect an uncritical heuristic for upward trends. People are not universally myopic and many genuinely value improving aggregate conditions retrospectively and prospectively.

articles.title: Calculation and Conscience: Motivations for the Substantive Representation of Ethnic Minorities
articles.authors: Stephanie Zonszein, Apurav Bhatiya, William Dinneen, Guy Grossman
articles.abstract: Existing work shows that minority legislators are more likely to represent their group’s interests compared to dominant group legislators. However, it is unclear whether this is due to intrinsic motivations or electoral incentives. We use a regression discontinuity design (RDD) to analyze ethnic minority representation in the UK Parliament. By comparing white MPs who narrowly beat minority candidates to minority MPs who narrowly beat white candidates, the RDD controls for electoral incentives since it holds constant constituency factors correlated with a minority parliamentary win. Analyzing over 1 million parliamentary questions and speeches, we find that minority MPs are more likely than white MPs to discuss issues important to ethnic minorities. Additional evidence suggests that narrowly elected MPs face similar electoral incentives and that minority MPs representing minorities face re-election penalties. Our findings are consistent with the idea that minority substantive representation is driven at least in part by intrinsic motivations.

Get out to deliberate (GOTD): Door-to-door canvassing to improve civic engagement
articles.authors: Katy Tabero, Zohreh Khoban, Paolo Spada, Rafael Mestre, Matt Ryan
articles.abstract: Several decades of experimentation have found that ‘Get-Out-the-Vote’ (GOTV) campaigns can effectively increase voter turnout. Yet, little has been said about the ability of similar-style campaigns to encourage participation in other types of civic engagement, such as citizens’ assemblies, which require much higher levels of commitment. Furthermore, although studies have found general support for citizens’ assemblies, willingness to participate is higher amongst those already more politically engaged and with higher levels of education, presenting a challenge to claims surrounding legitimacy and representation. In this article, we conduct a GOTV-style field experiment, complemented by a doorstep survey, to increase and understand perspectives towards registration for the 2023 Southampton Citizens’ Climate Assembly. We find that canvassing can be an effective method for increasing registration, including from under-represented groups. However, there are considerable barriers to participation, particularly the level of commitment, personal interest, and concerns about impact, which limit recruitment efforts.

articles.title: The rhetoric of responsibility in party manifestos (1980–2021)
articles.abstract: Focusing on the responsibility–responsiveness dilemma, we analyze responsibility rhetoric (defined as the emphasis on elements such as national solidarity, the public interest, and public-spiritedness), hypothesizing that it is used by parties moderating their policy positions, to justify deviations from their traditional standpoints, as well as by large incumbent parties seeking to claim credit for their responsible actions. In contrast, populist and niche parties, which prioritize responsiveness, are expected to avoid such rhetoric. We apply the manifestoberta Large Language Model (LLM) to classify natural sentences from up to 1,927 party manifestos (1980–2021), covering 38 countries worldwide, into the traditional MARPOR/Comparative Manifesto Project (CMP) coding categories. We then adopt two methods, a semisupervised Latent Dirichlet allocation topic model (Seeded-LDA) and the OpenAI GPT-4o-mini LLM, to refine one of these categories by selecting only those sentences that align with our concept of responsibility rhetoric. The results of statistical analysis support our hypotheses and are robust across different operationalizations of the dependent variable.

articles.title: Shared Discrimination’s Effect on Solidarity between People of Color Is Uniform Across Major Racial, Political, and Social Differences
articles.authors: Kasheena Rogbeer, Emily Ortiz, Efrén Pérez
articles.abstract: Solidarity between people of color (PoC) is key to understanding multiracial coalition-building in the United States. However, limited statistical power has constrained research on whether shared discrimination’s effect on solidarity is reliably moderated by differences in race, political orientation, and social background, which structure the internal diversity of racially stigmatized subgroups within the mega-category, PoC. We report a preregistered meta-analysis of eight published experiments ( N = 5,813), which used a common design to test shared discrimination’s effects among Black Americans, Asian Americans, Latinos, and Middle Eastern and North African individuals. Despite known heterogeneity in these group’s social and political attitudes, we find that shared discrimination’s effect on solidarity is statistically uniform across race/ethnicity, partisanship, ideology, nativity, education, gender, and age. These results indicate that shared discrimination appeals broadly and reliably activate solidarity across diverse PoC subgroups, further affirming this psychological mechanism’s crucial role in fostering robust multiracial coalitions.

articles.title: How preferential voting and party ideology shape campaign-focus in proportional electoral systems
articles.authors: Julius Lehtinen, Mikko Mattila, Åsa von Schoultz
articles.abstract: While electoral systems shape candidates’ incentives to cultivate personal reputations, institutional rules do not translate mechanically into campaign behaviour. We argue that both electoral institutions and ideological traditions shape campaign strategies: ideological traditions influence both the attractiveness of candidate-centred appeals and how strongly candidates respond to institutional incentives. We present the first large cross-national test of their joint influence, using data from 37 elections in 16 countries under proportional representation. We show that candidate-centred campaigning is more prevalent in open list systems, but that this institutional effect is not uniform. Candidates from leftleaning parties are more party-centred, and the personalising effect of open lists is weaker among them than among candidates from right leaning parties. These findings show that the consequences of electoral reform depend on the normative and strategic contexts in which parties operate.

articles.title: Re-electing the party leader: The 2024 PASOK contest
articles.abstract: This article examines leadership contests in European mainstream parties confronting electoral decline and attempting to restore competitiveness. Focusing on this broader phenomenon, it analyses incumbent leaders seeking renewed mandates through open primary elections in such contexts. The article applies Stark’s (1996) selection criteria (‘acceptability’, ‘electability’ and ‘competence’) to the 2024 Panhellenic Socialist Movement (PASOK) leadership contest in Greece as a demanding empirical and methodological setting: an incumbent leader seeking re-election through a competitive open primary within a recovery major party after only limited electoral improvement. Drawing on candidates’ speeches, press reports, official results and polling indicators mapped onto Stark’s criteria, the study evaluates party members’ and supporters’ perceptions of the main contenders. The findings show that the incumbent leader, Nikos Androulakis, led his opponents on all three criteria and suggest that incumbent re-election in recovery major parties is broadly consistent with Stark’s model when electability is interpreted as credible electoral recovery and unity concerns stem from strategic rather than ideological conflict.

articles.title: Correcting for Nonignorable Nonresponse Bias in Ordinal Observational Survey Data
articles.authors: Lukáš Lafférs, Jozef Michal Mintal, Ivan Sutóris
articles.abstract: Many political surveys rely on post-stratification, raking or related weighting adjustments to align respondents with the target population. But when respondents differ from nonrespondents on the outcome itself (nonignorable nonresponse), these adjustments can fail, introducing bias even into basic descriptives. We provide a practical method that corrects for nonignorable nonresponse by leveraging response-propensity proxies (e.g., a respondent’s rating of the interview or interviewer-coded cooperativeness) observed among respondents to extrapolate toward nonrespondents, while directly integrating observable covariates and retaining the benefits of post-stratification with known population shares. The method generalizes the variable-response-propensity framework of Peress (2010) from binary to ordinal outcomes, which are widely used to measure trust, satisfaction and policy attitudes. The resulting estimator is computed by maximum likelihood and implemented in a compact R routine that handles both ordinal and binary outcomes. Using the 2024 American National Election Study, we show that accounting for nonignorable nonresponse produces substantively meaningful shifts for life satisfaction (estimated latent correlation ρ ≈ 0.47 $\rho \approx 0.47$ rho almost equals 0.47 ), while yielding only modest changes for retrospective economic evaluations ( ρ ≈ 0.14 $\rho \approx 0.14$ rho almost equals 0.14 ), highlighting when nonignorable nonresponse substantively affects survey estimates.

articles.title: Cool Citizens? How Affectively Unpolarized Citizens View and Participate in Democracy
articles.authors: Peter Luca Versteegen, Joseph B. Phillips, Lilliana Mason
articles.abstract: Does affective polarization change how citizens view and participate in democracy? We posit that the answer to this crucial question depends on how affectively un polarized citizens view and participate in democracy. Yet, the most common operationalization of affective polarization––measuring sympathy ratings for one party relative to another––does not differentiate between people’s absolute sympathy ratings for the parties, which may mask essential heterogeneity among unpolarized citizens. This paper theorizes the methodological origin of this heterogeneity, describes it, and highlights its implications. Cluster analyses and regressions from three nationally representative surveys in the US provide three conclusions. First, substantial shares of the US population are affectively un polarized. Second, unpolarized citizens cluster into two groups: one feeling lukewarm and one feeling cold toward both parties. Third, these unpolarized groups report diverging democratic attitudes and participation patterns. We discuss the methodological implications and the need for future research on affectively unpolarized citizens.

articles.title: Women Politicians’ Role Model Effects: The Influence of Shared Identities Beyond Gender
articles.abstract: Women consistently report lower levels of political interest and political ambition than men. Studies have examined how women politicians as role models can make women more politically engaged, but studies have not typically examined additional shared identities beyond gender. I propose that women politicians with whom women share additional identities will be perceived as more relatable and inspiring and, consequently, have stronger role model effects on women’s political engagement. Through a conjoint experiment (Study 1), I find that having additional shared identities with a woman politician increases perceptions of her as relatable and inspiring. However, a survey experiment with novel video treatments depicting a woman politician’s story (Study 2) did not produce positive role model effects on women’s political interest, internal political efficacy, or nascent political ambition – regardless of additional shared racial and partisan identity with the woman politician. Moreover, the video treatment had remarkably different effects across White and Black women, regardless of additional shared racial and partisan identity. An observational analysis (Study 3) replicates the finding that additional shared racial and partisan identity with women political representatives is not systematically correlated with higher levels of political interest. These findings carry important implications for understanding women politicians’ role model effects and the potential of role models to increase women’s political engagement.

High accuracy with low costs: the pretrain-finetune paradigm for classification with transformer-based language models
articles.abstract: Political science increasingly uses text classification to gauge subtle concepts such as toxicity or anger. Traditional methods treat words in isolation, overlooking the contextual dynamics where meaning resides. Transformer-based language models address these limitations but remain underutilized, especially among applied scholars, partly due to misconceptions about their mechanisms and computational requirements. This article bridges this gap by offering an accessible explication of the pretrain-finetune paradigm, focusing on underlying mechanisms and their potential to improve political text analysis by harnessing models trained on extensive datasets while requiring modest labeled data and computational resources. I demonstrate the approach by identifying toxic language in conversation threads following U.S. Senators’ tweets and provide an online tutorial to support nontechnical scholars in adopting the methodology.

articles.title: Does preference intensity matter? Reexamining policy representation in the American states
articles.authors: Zachary Peskowitz, Eddy S. F. Yeung
articles.abstract: Preference intensity may play an important role in shaping mass political behavior, yet existing empirical scholarship on representation typically relies on survey measures that capture public opinion in terms of preference directionality without intensity. We use a variety of measures—not only the standard Likert and “most important policy” items but also the quadratic voting method—to reassess responsiveness and congruence of a diverse set of American state policies that vary in issue areas and salience. Across multiple novel measures of individual policy preferences, we consistently find that state-level preference intensity does not reliably predict actual policy outcomes. We contribute new evidence that the lack of policy representation in the American states remains—even if preference intensity is systematically integrated into the empirical analysis.

articles.title: Populism and academic freedom
articles.abstract: Academic freedom empowers scholars to influence public discourse and debate, cultivate critical reasoning, discuss ideas that challenge traditional values, and impose a soft check and balance on governments. For those reasons, governments have specific preferences regarding the extent of academic freedom, especially when led by populists, whose ideology, values, and strategic features are frequently at odds with the implications of this freedom. Using a quasi-experimental design, we confirm that academic freedom declines significantly under populist governments, a pattern largely independent of their host ideology. Those negative consequences increase after multiple populist terms, and extend more broadly to the substance of speech and the flow of information. Altogether, these results highlight the incompatibility of populism with democratic guarantees.

articles.title: Discretionary disclosure and electoral accountability
articles.abstract: Politicians often have discretion over what policy information to reveal to the public. This paper develops a formal model comparing electoral accountability under mandatory and discretionary disclosure. I identify a fundamental trade-off between detection − where voters directly observe wrongdoing − and inference − where voters penalize the suspicious absence of information. Mandates facilitate detection but eliminate the strategic signal embedded in discretionary disclosure. Mandates weaken the connection between silence and possible wrongdoing, effectively exonerating the incumbent in voters’ inferences. The model demonstrates that when the baseline probability of information transmission is high, the inference-based mechanism constrains rent-seeking more effectively than the detection-based mechanism. Consequently, disclosure mandates can paradoxically weaken electoral discipline: by making silence less informative, they undermine voters’ ability to draw inferences from silence, even while increasing the overall probability that voters observe policy outcomes.

articles.title: What does the public know about their State’s abortion laws in the post-Dobbs era?
articles.authors: Marisa Abrajano, Marianna Garcia, Aaron Pope, Robert Vidigal, Jonathan Nagler
articles.abstract: Following the Dobbs decision in the U.S., there were widespread reports of misinformation regarding the ruling. Many Americans may therefore have faced uncertainty about abortion laws in their state, and Latinos—approximately 40% of whom are foreign-born—may be particularly vulnerable due to limited familiarity with the U.S. political system. To better understand awareness of state abortion policies, we fielded a national online panel survey containing large samples of Latinos ( N = 2326) and non-Hispanic whites ( N = 769). We find that Latinos were 6 percentage points less likely to correctly identify their state’s abortion law relative to white Americans and were 10.7 percentage points more likely to overestimate the strictness of those laws, even when controlling for demographic, religious, and political covariates. Foreign-born Latinos were also 19.5 percentage points more likely to overestimate the strictness of their state’s abortion law compared to their U.S.-born counterparts. These findings contribute to our understanding of differential learning following sudden policy change and highlight significant knowledge gaps that may affect whether individuals seek abortion care if they misunderstand the legal status in their state. Such gaps may have downstream consequences for health care access and economic inequality.
